subject: economics
title: Price Controls
welcome_lead: Maximum and minimum prices - well-intentioned, often distorting.
meta_desc: A-Level Government Intervention: price ceilings and floors.
final_note: Price controls create shortages or surpluses by overriding the market.

concepts.def: Result of a binding price ceiling.
Result of a binding price floor.
Classic price ceiling on housing rents.

walkthroughs.body_html: A binding ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage. Buyers queue, sellers may cut quality, black markets emerge. Rent controls are the classic case.
A binding floor above equilibrium creates a surplus. Minimum wages may cause unemployment if labour demand is elastic; agricultural floors leave butter mountains.
Despite distortions, ceilings can protect consumers in emergencies and floors can support producer incomes. The right answer depends on alternatives and elasticities.

options: Surplus
Shortage
Equilibrium
Higher tax revenue

mcqs.q: Minimum wage above equilibrium can cause:
options: Labour shortage
Unemployment if labour demand is elastic
Lower inflation always
Surplus of jobs

mcqs.q: What is the predicted effect of a binding price ceiling like rent control?
options: Price ceilings make goods cheaper for everyone with no downsides.
Price ceilings only affect the rich.
Shortage in the market — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price, leading to queues, black markets and reduced quality.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A minimum wage is paid by the government.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What does standard theory predict about a minimum wage?
options: A minimum wage is paid by the government.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
A minimum wage always reduces unemployment because workers have more money to spend.
If above equilibrium, it raises wages for those still employed but causes unemployment by reducing labour demand — though empirical evidence is mixed.
